BEST JAZZ The Best Jazz on Bandcamp, June 2026 By Dave Sumner · June 30, 2026

The strength of a particular month’s releases is not always best reflected by the first batch of recommendations, but by those included in the “Other Albums of Note” section. This month, all of the albums included there wholeheartedly deserved a more prominent spot on this column—a few more words of advocacy—but there’s only so much space before I have to make an anguished decision. So, start at the top of this column, start at the end, any direction you go is gonna lead to some excellent new music. Find your spot, and let’s begin.

The influences of the masterpiece from Mariam Wallentin and Vestnorsk Jazzensemble is a mixture of modern jazz, poetry, classical, folk, post-rock, and experimental, with each influence tightly bound to its counterparts, but never subsuming the others. Each influence stands out alone, together. Wallentin’s vocals wind through a dectet of strings, wind instruments, percussion, and electric guitars, the music remaining ephemeral while simultaneously digging into a groove—rising up with intensity and maintaining a peaceful drone, a thing of beauty and power. The album’s genesis traces back to Wallentin’s stay in Basel, and the experience of nesting along the Rhine in springtime. This album only could’ve been released on Hubro.

Where previous recordings from Soojin Suh revolved around the melodic expression, the latest from the Seoul-based drummer is all about rhythmic flexibility and reinvention. Joined by double bassist Hoo Kim and pianist Jaehun Kang, Suh considers the piano trio through the lens of the drummer, toying with traditional roles within that dynamic and conventional ways of playing out of it. An album like Colorist was likely to enthrall the listener; Prism of Existence engages them fully, to the point where there’s no breaking free.

The inspiration for the latest from Miles Okazaki came as he was driving through Wyoming. The guitarist is drawn to the concept of distinct American imagery and the conflicted emotional reactions they’re capable of triggering, and the Wyoming landscape spoke to that. Wyoming will do that to you: there are landscapes that are jaw-dropping for their immensity yet also elicit an unsettling feeling at their emptiness, summoning the idea that “life has abandoned this place.” Boomtown turns those emotions into music. Joined by an all-star cast of nine, Okazaki’s music is a simultaneous view through two different lenses—one that captures a wide frame perspective from above, and the other that gets to the heart of things at a granular level. The music is often volatile, sometimes wistful. It has a multi-directional focus, as if the forces of chaos and structure formed an uneasy alliance just for this recording.

The latest from Nils Berg—a collaboration with Sweden’s Norrbotten Big Band—uses the concept of a professional mourner as inspiration. What I found most intriguing about this theme is the idea of composition versus improvisation, and how the professional mourner likely relies on the scripted emotional demeanor to lead to spontaneous—even heartfelt—expressions. This music lands with plenty of emotional impact, leading out with harmonic resonance and interspersing it with melodic tenderness. It’s yet one more compelling thematic device from the wind instrumentalist. This is a rare opportunity to purchase something from the excellent, criminally under-the-radar label HOOB Records. And speaking of HOOB: if Nils Berg’s Cinemascope recordings ever land on Bandcamp, I strongly encourage you to download them immediately. 2011’s Popmotion and 2016’s Searching for Amazing Talent From Punjab are never far from my thoughts.

The music of Helen Svoboda sets up camp at the fringes of modern jazz, and isn’t opposed to running into territories even further remote. With Headwater, Svoboda sought to expand on her double bass-vocals-electronics solo sound, and hiring a vocalist, a double bassist, and an electronic effects person to duplicate, amplify, and morph that sound, posed an intriguing question of identity: Where did Svoboda end and the collaborating musicians begin? Joined by vocalist Selma Savolainen (Finnish, like Svoboda), double bassist Jacques Emery, and electronics specialist (and producer) Tilman Robinson, there’s a heady blend of avant-garde and folk jazz, a sweet spot where conflict and resolution aren’t necessarily linear nor easily differentiated. Further highlighting Svoboda’s borderless expressionism, the bassist also just released a new one with her Meatshell duo with Andrew Saragossi.

Seeing as how Gary Bartz has been at the center of Jazz’s various stages of evolution over the decades, it’s only natural to find the saxophonist collaborating with the sextet Your Brother’s Keeper. What’s new is Bartz’s medium. The tides shift on the influences present on Where Rivers Meet—some cosmic jazz, some spiritual jazz, some contemporary post-bop—but all are sufficiently downstream to seem detached from the nascent stages of Bartz’s earlier years, and more akin to the new thing from the London scene. Tuneful and tranquil, equal doses, served generously.

There’s a lot of different parts on this trio set from drummer Giovanni Nardiello, pianist Joseph Nowell, and double bassist Stefano Zambon, and those parts rarely stay still for long. Often they’re wrapped up in melodies that display a tuneful pop music aesthetic. The trio digs into a groove as frequently as they scatter like marbles, and no matter where a passage is situated along that spectrum, the resulting motion is as delightful as it is fun. Noemi Fiorucci adds guest vocals on about half of the album’s tracks, providing a dose of harmonic gravitas to balance things out. This music isn’t straight-forward, but enjoying it certainly is.

There might not be an instrument better able to capture the turmoil of contemplative moments than Nate Wooley’s trumpet. When unleashed, Wooley’s trumpet is the sound of something having traveled a very long distance across difficult terrain. It is both contemplation and turmoil that frames the latest from Wooley’s Columbia Icefield, and the feeling of absence after death. A Silence Opens centered originally on the music and musician Ron Miles, a collaborator and friend of Wooley’s who’d passed away four years ago. But then, sadly, the scope of that absence expanded with the passing of ensemble member Susan Alcorn shortly after this session was recorded. Wooley, pedal steel guitarist Alcorn, guitarist Ava Mendoza, and drummer Ryan Sawyer, plus a choir adopt three Ron Miles compositions as their own, in addition to Wooley originals, and offer up music that captures all of the emotion one would imagine such a project might convey. It’s powerful music outside of the context, emotionally intense in light of it.

A nice straight-ahead post-bop session from the trio of tenor saxophonist Mark Turner, bassist Joe Martin, and drummer Marcus Gilmore. The trio keeps things typically upbeat, canting along at a brisk pace, and the chatter they develop individually melts pleasantly into a fluid, unified dialogue. However, I’d argue that the strongest moments are when they grow more deliberate with the melodicism and let thoughts hang in the air, lingering for an extra few moments, before bringing them to a conclusion. There’s a sweet tension that comes out of that, and it was the tracks that had me returning for another listen. Opening track “The Fencer” is Exhibit A in that regard.

It’s a meditative experience delivered by the duo of Peggy Buard and Émilie Chevillard—the former on chromatic and prepared harps and the latter on piano, including prepared. In many ways—all of them good—Dyade reflects the music released by Yolk Records. There’s a strong folk music aspect to the modern jazz expressionism, though exactly to where that jazz element traces its roots is elusive. Chamber music, or in the spirit of. Daring experimentalism, following textural and rhythmic paths that lead to surprising places. And always a heavy emphasis on melodic depth or narrative integrity. You’ll become entranced either by the individual notes and phrases or the story they tell.

This is the kind of recording where sudden strikes of emotional impact leave you wondering, “Where the hell did that come from?” This duo session from trumpeter Kris Tiner and pianist Cathlene Pineda is built on some weighty feelings, so it’s little wonder that it would have a similar impact on its listeners. Even those pieces that have something akin to an upbeat or overactive behavior—like “New Build” and “Something Has Shifted”—radiate tones heavy with introspection. If the moon is hanging outside your window as you listen, it was this album’s gravitational pull that brought it into your orbit.

The sextet Microfiche straddles the borders between modern jazz and post-rock, a place where structure is the byproduct of living one melodic moment to the next. There’s never any sense of beginning and end, just blinking into existence and back out. It’s music that’s easy to immerse oneself in and drift away; the harmonic inventiveness is how the sextet jars the listener back to a state of heightened awareness. Tones are conducive to introspective interludes, though there are certainly times when things reach a boil. Trumpet, saxophones, clarinets, piano & keyboards, electric & acoustic basses, drums & percussion are the instruments of choice, with economical use of electronic effects done just right.

Other Albums of Note:

Column fixtures Ambrose Akinmusire, Mary Halvorson, and James Brandon Lewis all have new albums out this month—Akinmusire and Halvorson in a duet (released on Nonesuch) and JBL with his quartet (on Intakt Records). While a rendition of Monk’s “Locomotive” reveals a fine match with the Willber Sunlight quartet of saxophonist Kevin Sun, guitarist Max Light, bassist Simón Willson, and drummer Aaron Seeber, ultimately it’s their original compositions that win the day (released on Endectomorph Music). Lots of raw melodicism on this highly expressive session from Ilaria Capalbo, with the double bassist’s interactions with the bass clarinet of Thomas Backman as one of the major highlights. There’s a delightful mix of classic hard bop, cosmic funk, and spy thriller soundtrack on the new release from Freyja Garbett (released on Earshift Music). And we’re ending the column with Tejido by Daniel González Rodríguez—a rec for the jazz guitar fan and an album that may be the under-the-radar gem of June—with warm tones, lively rhythmic dialogue, and a rich melodicism, as the guitarist intertwines his Columbian and Jazz music roots into one strand.
